instructions: Speak confidently and conversationally, like a senior product manager giving a live technical demo to an engineering audience. Clear enunciation, steady medium pace, warm but precise. Light inflection on key terms. No hype, no salesiness, no pauses between sentences. Flow naturally from one thought to the next.

scenes.title: Ask BC — an AI operator for your BigCommerce store
scenes.caption: This is Ask BC, a chat surface that connects to a BigCommerce store through a Cloudflare Worker running Project Think. The merchant types a question. The agent writes TypeScript, executes it in a sandboxed Dynamic Worker, and streams real React components inline — not markdown tables, real UI. Five suggested questions, a text input, and a green dot showing the WebSocket is live.

scenes.title: KPI summary — five metrics in one shot
scenes.caption: The merchant asks for a store summary. The agent writes one TypeScript script that calls getProducts, getCustomers, getOrderCount, and getOrders in parallel, aggregates total revenue and average order value in memory, and returns five KPI cards. One hundred nineteen products, one hundred twenty-seven customers, forty-seven orders, eighty-one thousand dollars in revenue, seventeen hundred dollar average order value. Six point six seconds, Haiku four-point-five, one execute.

scenes.title: Structured tables — typed columns, real data
scenes.caption: Next question: most expensive products. The agent emits a DataTable component with typed columns — product name, SKU, price right-aligned, inventory right-aligned. Five rows of real catalog data from the BigCommerce V3 API. The model sorted by price in memory because the API's sort enum doesn't include price. Five point five seconds.

scenes.title: Three-way join — orders, line items, customers
scenes.caption: Now the hard question: show me my five most recent completed orders with line items and customer info. On the old tool-loop stack this was impossible — it would chain seven serial tool calls and hit the step cap. Here the agent writes one script that fetches completed orders, fans out getOrderProducts for each, joins in memory, and returns a structured table with per-line-item detail. Product name, quantity, unit price, line total — all real data from three different API surfaces joined in a single sandbox execution.

scenes.title: Write operations — the merchant asks for a change
scenes.caption: The merchant types: create a coupon called WINTER twenty for twenty percent off. This isn't a read. The agent identifies the intent, selects the createCoupon tool, and emits the tool call with typed arguments: name, code, type percentage discount, amount twenty, enabled true. No codemode sandbox this time — writes are top-level tools that execute directly with the real BC access token.

scenes.title: Write confirmation — verified in BigCommerce
scenes.caption: The coupon is created. The WriteApproval card shows EXECUTED with a green confirmation strip — change applied to your store. Below it, the agent summarizes: code WINTER twenty, discount twenty percent off, scope store-wide, status enabled. This isn't hallucinated. The BigCommerce V2 coupons API returned two-oh-one Created, and the agent read the response to build the summary. We verified it directly: curl to the coupons endpoint, id two, code WINTER twenty, amount twenty, enabled true.

scenes.title: Why Codemode matters
scenes.caption: Under the hood, every read question follows the same pattern. The model writes TypeScript. The TypeScript runs in a Dynamic Worker sandbox with zero network access — the only way out is codemode-dot-star RPC calls that resolve to typed tool functions in the host worker. The host holds the BigCommerce access token. The sandbox never sees it. This is the same credential isolation architecture Cloudflare uses in Agent Lee.

scenes.title: Two models — speed where it's cheap, power where it counts
scenes.caption: Haiku four-point-five handles every normal chat turn including in-turn error recovery. Three times cheaper, two-point-six times faster than Sonnet. Sonnet four-point-six activates automatically on continuation turns — post-approval write execution and chat recovery after a Durable Object restart. The merchant gets fast answers on reads, deep reasoning on writes. Both models share the same typed tool surface.

scenes.title: Six generative UI components
scenes.caption: The agent doesn't output markdown and hope the client formats it. It emits fenced code blocks with language 'block' containing typed JSON — KPI cards, data tables, product cards, order timelines, inventory bars, sparkline charts. The Next.js client parses these and mounts real React components inline. Each component is styled to match BigDesign, the BigCommerce admin component library, so the output feels native to the control panel.

scenes.title: The architecture — hybrid Vercel plus Cloudflare
scenes.caption: Next.js on Vercel handles OAuth install, JWT sessions, the iframe shell, and App Extensions registration. The Cloudflare Worker handles the agent runtime — Project Think as the base class, Codemode for execution, a Durable Object per store for session persistence, and Dynamic Workers for sandboxed code execution. The browser connects directly to the Worker via WebSocket. Credentials stay in the Durable Object — generated code in the sandbox never touches them.

scenes.title: Typed BigCommerce SDK — fifteen read tools, four write tools
scenes.caption: Eleven OpenAPI specs pulled from BigCommerce's public docs repo, run through openapi-typescript to generate thirty-five thousand lines of typed definitions. Fifteen read tools cover products, variants, categories, brands, orders, order line items, shipping addresses, customers, inventory locations, promotions, coupons, and channels. Four write tools for coupon creation, inventory adjustment, product visibility, and price updates. All backed by openapi-fetch with typed path validation.

scenes.title: Your store, operating itself
scenes.caption: That's Ask BC. A chat surface over the store's real APIs, with generative UI components that render platform-native, write operations that mutate store state, and a Codemode execution model that turns every question into a single TypeScript script. The merchant doesn't learn a new tool. They just tell the store what they want, and the store does it.
